\chapter{Asking For It}
\label{ch:ml-venam}
\hlchaptermodality{76}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask somebody whether they want something.}

From cold: offer tea, and give both answers -- the acceptance and the refusal the track already had.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vēṇō]{\ml{വേണോ} (vēṇō) — \textquotedblleft{}do you want?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C76-veno}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{wanted}. Then say the one letter Malayalam puts on the end of something to turn it into a question.

Put them together before you read on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വേണോ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ചായ} \ml{വേണോ}?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{cāya vēṇō?} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Do you want tea?}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

If you built \textbf{\ml{വേണോ}} in the warm-up, this lesson taught you nothing, which is the point. \textbf{\ml{വേണം}} loses its ending and takes the question letter you already had, and that is the whole derivation.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a three-way set you now own}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വേണോ}?} & do you want it? \\
\textbf{\ml{വേണം}} & yes — wanted \\
\textbf{\ml{വേണ്ട}} & no — not wanted \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{That is a whole exchange.} One person offers, the other accepts or declines, and every word in it is a form of the same root.

Notice which one arrived first. The track gave you \textbf{the refusal} long before the request, so for a while you could say no to an offer you had no way of making. Both halves are yours now.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cāya vēṇō?}
  \item both answers — \emph{vēṇaṁ}, then \emph{vēṇṭa}
  \item the offer with water instead of tea
  \item which letter turned the statement into the question
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you offer somebody tea? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{ചായ} \ml{വേണോ}?}}) How do you accept? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{വേണം}}}.) And how do you decline? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{വേണ്ട}}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vēṇaṁ ōrmma]{(wanted, and not) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R76-want-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{wanted} and \emph{not wanted}, and hear how much of the two words is the same.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one root, a whole exchange}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ചായ} \ml{വേണോ}?} & do you want tea? \\
\textbf{\ml{വേണം}} & yes \\
\textbf{\ml{വേണ്ട}} & no \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three words, one root, and the shortest complete conversation this book has given you. \textbf{Only one of the three was new this chapter} — the question form you can build yourself, and the acceptance the refusal had been pointing at all along.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The ability to \textbf{ask for something}, which needs one more thing said about it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{വെള്ളം} \ml{വേണം}.}
\end{quote}

\emph{To me, water is wanted.} \textbf{You are not the subject of your own wanting} — the water is. That is the same shape knowing and age already took, and it is the habit to carry forward: when something happens \emph{to} a person in Malayalam, the person goes in the dative and the thing goes to the front.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item offer tea, accept, then decline
  \item \emph{enikku veḷḷaṁ vēṇaṁ}
  \item who the subject of that sentence is
  \item the three forms in the order an exchange uses them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Offer somebody water. (\emph{\textbf{\ml{വെള്ളം} \ml{വേണോ}?}}) Accept it. (\emph{\textbf{\ml{വേണം}}}.) And in \emph{enikku veḷḷaṁ vēṇaṁ}, who is the subject? (\textbf{The water}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
